title: The Nuclear Envelope and Nuclear Transport

generated.pipeline: extract -> Codex draft -> Codex accuracy gate and fix

cards.front: Why must an ordinary eukaryotic cell support traffic both into and out of the nucleus?
cards.back: Soluble nuclear proteins are made in the cytosol, whereas messenger RNA and ribosomal subunits made inside the nucleus must leave.
cards.quote: soluble nuclear proteins are synthesized on cytosolic ribosomes, while messenger RNA and ribosomal subunits made inside must leave

cards.front: In animal cells, the inner and outer nuclear membranes are about {{c1::20 to 40 nm}} apart.
cards.quote: The nuclear envelope's inner and outer lipid bilayers are described as about 20 to 40 nm apart in animal cells.

cards.front: Why is the perinuclear space topologically part of the ER lumen?
cards.back: The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER membrane, so the perinuclear space connects to ER lumen without crossing a membrane.
cards.quote: The outer membrane is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum, so the perinuclear space between them is ER lumen

cards.front: A soluble tracer is placed in the perinuclear space. Without crossing a membrane, where can it go: cytosol, nucleoplasm, or ER lumen? What happens and why?
cards.back: It reaches the ER lumen because that lumen is continuous with the perinuclear space. The pore instead connects cytosol with nucleoplasm.
cards.quote: It and the perinuclear space are topologically equivalent: they are continuous without crossing a membrane.

cards.front: The {{c1::nuclear lamina}} is a lamin meshwork that mechanically stabilizes the nucleus and bridges the envelope and chromatin.
cards.quote: the lamina, a lamin meshwork that gives the nucleus mechanical stability and bridges envelope and chromatin

cards.front: What is the basic architecture of a nuclear pore scaffold?
cards.back: It has eightfold symmetry and contains multiple copies of roughly 30 kinds of nucleoporin.
cards.quote: Each pore has an eightfold-symmetric scaffold built from multiple copies of roughly 30 kinds of nucleoporin.

cards.front: Disordered nucleoporin domains with {{c1::phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats}} line the pore channel and form its selective barrier.
cards.quote: Nucleoporins with disordered phenylalanine-glycine, or FG, repeats line the channel and form its selective barrier.

cards.front: For exponential nuclear exchange, the fraction of excess signal remaining is {{c1::x(t) / x(0) = exp(-t / τ)}}.
cards.quote: Model that excess as one exponential: x(t) / x(0) = exp(-t / τ)

cards.front: Why is the nuclear pore called a soft barrier rather than a sharp size cutoff?
cards.back: Passive permeability falls steeply and continuously as size increases; larger reporters exchange slowly rather than being absolutely excluded.
cards.quote: Passive permeability falls steeply but continuously with size: this is a soft barrier, not a cutoff.

cards.front: For reporters with τ = 15 s and τ = 413 s, what fractions of excess nuclear signal remain after 60 s?
cards.back: Use exp(-t/τ). exp(-60/15) = exp(-4) = 0.018, so 1.8% remains; exp(-60/413) = 0.865, so 86.5% remains.
cards.why: The 67 kDa reporter has not relaxed by half after one minute, whereas the 27 kDa GFP reporter is almost at equilibrium.
cards.quote: Their normalized time constants were τ = 15 s for 27 kDa GFP and τ = 413 s for a 67 kDa reporter.

cards.front: What are the half-times for exponential exchange with τ = 15 s and τ = 413 s?
cards.back: Use t½ = τ ln 2. The half-times are 15(0.693) = 10.4 s and 413(0.693) = 286 s.
cards.quote: The half-time is t½ = τ × ln 2.

cards.front: An excess nuclear signal falls to 25% of its initial value in 120 s. Assuming x(t)/x(0) = exp(-t/τ), what is τ?
cards.quote: Model that excess as one exponential: x(t) / x(0) = exp(-t / τ)

cards.front: A reporter's mass rises from 27 to 67 kDa while its exchange time constant rises from 15 to 413 s. What do the ratios show about the pore barrier?
cards.back: Mass rises 67/27 = 2.48-fold and τ rises 413/15 = 27.5-fold. Size sharply slows exchange but does not stop it, supporting a soft barrier.
cards.why: This combines the quantitative comparison with the observation that the larger reporter still exchanges.
cards.quote: A 2.5-fold rise in mass (67/27 = 2.48) increased the time constant about 27-fold (413/15 = 27.5), yet did not stop exchange.

cards.front: Why should an exchange time constant not be interpreted as one molecule's transit time through one nuclear pore?
cards.back: The measured value describes relaxation of excess signal across an entire yeast nucleus, not a single molecule's dwell time in one pore.
cards.quote: These values describe relaxation of excess signal in a yeast nucleus, not the time one molecule spends in one pore.

cards.front: A classical nuclear localization signal is a {{c1::basic amino-acid sequence recognized by importin α}}.
cards.quote: A classical nuclear localization signal (NLS) is a basic amino-acid sequence recognized by importin α.
cards.section: Signals: what an experiment can prove

cards.front: What happens to a classical NLS after its protein enters the nucleus, and what consequence follows?
cards.back: It ordinarily remains part of the protein rather than being cut off, so it can support import again later.
cards.quote: Unlike many ER signal sequences in protein sorting, it is ordinarily not cut off.
cards.section: Signals: what an experiment can prove

cards.front: How do importin α and importin β connect a classical NLS cargo to the nuclear pore?
cards.back: Importin α binds the NLS, importin β binds importin α, and importin β engages FG repeats in the pore.
cards.quote: importin α binds the NLS, importin β binds importin α, and importin β engages FG repeats in the pore
cards.section: Signals: what an experiment can prove

cards.front: A nuclear export signal recognized by CRM1 is a pattern of {{c1::spaced hydrophobic residues, often leucines}}.
cards.quote: A nuclear export signal (NES) recognized by CRM1, also called exportin 1, is a pattern of spaced hydrophobic residues, often leucines.
cards.section: Signals: what an experiment can prove

cards.front: Tail-less nucleoplasmin cores stay cytoplasmic after cytoplasmic injection but stay nuclear after nuclear injection; a larger one-tail pentamer enters from the cytoplasm. What does this show?
cards.back: The tail carries entry information distinct from retention. The larger one-tail pentamer also argues that size alone does not determine passage.
cards.quote: Tail-less cores injected into Xenopus oocyte cytoplasm stayed out; a larger one-tail pentamer entered.

cards.front: Suppose tail-less nucleoplasmin cores had been tested only by cytoplasmic injection and stayed cytoplasmic. What alternative explanation would remain, and why?
cards.back: They might have entered and then leaked back out. Nuclear injection is needed to show that the cores are retained, separating failed entry from failed retention.
cards.quote: Without the nuclear injection, a cytoplasmic core might have entered and leaked back out.

cards.front: Nucleoplasmin-coated gold is seen at nuclear pores, while gold with transport-deficient nucleoplasmin or inert-polymer coats is largely excluded. What do the observations establish?
cards.back: Transported cargo uses pores, and entry depends on a transport-competent protein coat rather than on the gold particle itself.
cards.quote: Transport-deficient nucleoplasmin or inert-polymer coatings were largely excluded, showing that entry depended on a transport-competent coat, not gold itself.

cards.front: An SV40 signal region makes two cytoplasmic reporters nuclear, but a one-residue signal mutant does not. What is supported, and what is not established by transfer alone?
cards.back: The sequence is sufficient for nuclear accumulation in those reporters, and that residue matters. Transfer alone does not prove necessity in the original protein or direct importin α binding.
cards.quote: The sequence is sufficient for nuclear accumulation in those reporters, and that residue matters.

cards.front: Ran is a small GTPase that is {{c1::on with GTP and off with GDP}}.
cards.quote: Ran is a small GTPase that works like the switches in GTPase switches: on with GTP and off with GDP.

cards.front: Why is receptor-assisted passage through a nuclear pore described as facilitated diffusion?
cards.back: The receptor speeds diffusive passage through the pore; it does not deliver an energy-powered stroke across the pore.
cards.quote: a receptor speeds diffusive passage through the pore rather than delivering a power stroke

cards.front: How can pore crossing require no power stroke while repeated directional nuclear accumulation still requires energy?
cards.back: Crossing is facilitated diffusion, but energy is needed to maintain the Ran gradient and reset receptors for repeated transport rounds.
cards.quote: Repeated directional accumulation still requires energy to maintain and reset the Ran system.

cards.front: How does RanGTP control cargo binding and release by importins?
cards.back: Importins load cargo where RanGTP is low in the cytoplasm and release cargo when RanGTP binds in the nucleus.
cards.quote: Importins load cargo where RanGTP is low, in the cytoplasm, and release it when nuclear RanGTP binds.

cards.front: How does RanGTP control cargo binding and release by exportins such as CRM1?
cards.back: Exportins bind cargo together with RanGTP in the nucleus and release it in the cytoplasm after complex disassembly and GTP hydrolysis.
cards.quote: Exportins such as CRM1 bind cargo only together with RanGTP in the nucleus and release it in the cytoplasm

cards.front: RanGAP1 is introduced into an oocyte nucleus, eliminating nuclear RanGTP. What happens to importin α/β-mediated import, and why?
cards.back: Import is inhibited because cargo cannot be properly unloaded in the nucleus and receptors cannot complete productive transport cycles.
cards.quote: Major import and export pathways stopped, export more readily than import.

cards.front: Transportin cargo crosses pores without Ran or nucleotide, but sustained accumulation requires Ran and hydrolysable GTP. What mechanistic distinction does this establish?
cards.back: Pore passage itself needs no energy-consuming stroke. Ran-dependent cargo release and GTP hydrolysis reset the receptor and support repeated directional rounds.
cards.quote: transportin, another import receptor, carried cargo across pores without Ran or nucleotide

cards.front: Why should the Ran-dependent transport rules not be applied to all messenger RNA export?
cards.back: Most messenger RNA exits through NXF1/TAP largely independently of Ran; spliced mRNA export continued without Ran in an oocyte assay.
cards.quote: Most messenger RNA leaves through NXF1, also called TAP, largely independently of Ran

cards.front: A transcription factor's NLS becomes masked while the protein remains intact. What happens to its nuclear import, and why?
cards.back: Import decreases because the receptor can no longer access the NLS. Re-exposing the signal can restore import without synthesizing a new protein.
cards.quote: Cells can also regulate import, for example by masking or exposing an NLS, to switch transcription factors on or off

cards.front: Chromatin-bound {{c1::RCC1}} loads GTP onto Ran, producing RanGTP in the nucleus.
cards.quote: RCC1, Ran's exchange factor, sits on chromatin and loads GTP onto Ran, making RanGTP in the nucleus.

cards.front: How do RCC1 and RanGAP1 create RanGTP asymmetry across the nuclear envelope?
cards.back: Chromatin-bound RCC1 loads Ran with GTP in the nucleus; cytoplasmic RanGAP1 stimulates hydrolysis, keeping cytoplasmic RanGTP low.
cards.quote: Cytoplasmic RanGAP1, helped by RanBP1, stimulates hydrolysis and keeps cytoplasmic RanGTP low.

cards.front: {{c1::NTF2}} returns RanGDP to the nucleus.
cards.quote: NTF2 returns RanGDP to the nucleus.

cards.front: How are importin α and importin β recycled after classical nuclear import?
cards.back: RanGTP separates β from α; Nup50 helps α release cargo. Importin β returns with RanGTP, while CAS returns α with RanGTP.
cards.quote: Importin β returns with RanGTP, while CAS returns α with RanGTP.

cards.front: How is a cytoplasmic CRM1-cargo-RanGTP export complex dismantled?
cards.back: RanBP1 helps dismantle the complex, then RanGAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis frees the receptor.
cards.quote: RanBP1 helps dismantle cytoplasmic CRM1-cargo-RanGTP before RanGAP-stimulated hydrolysis frees the receptor.

cards.front: Protein Z is cytoplasmic at steady state but becomes nuclear within an hour after leptomycin B is added. What is the simplest interpretation, and what remains unproved?
cards.back: Z normally enters and undergoes CRM1-dependent export, so blocking export reveals import. The result does not prove that Z has its own NLS or binds CRM1 directly.
cards.quote: Leptomycin B inhibits CRM1-dependent export. Protein Z is cytoplasmic at steady state in cultured cells, but within an hour of adding the drug it is nuclear.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: How would you test whether a candidate leucine-rich NES is necessary for Protein Z's cytoplasmic localization, and what result is predicted?
cards.back: Mutate key hydrophobic residues. If the NES is necessary, Z becomes nuclear without drug; verify expression, folding, and partner binding to exclude indirect disruption.
cards.quote: Mutate key hydrophobic residues in a candidate leucine-rich signal. Z should become nuclear without drug.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: How would you test whether a candidate basic cluster is Protein Z's main NLS, and what result is predicted under leptomycin B?
cards.back: Mutate the cluster. If it is the main entry route, Z remains cytoplasmic even with leptomycin B; residual entry could use another signal, a partner, or diffusion.
cards.quote: If it is Z's main route in, Z should stay cytoplasmic even with leptomycin B.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: How can a large, slowly diffusing inert reporter test whether Protein Z's candidate NLS and NES are sufficient?
cards.back: Attach each signal to the reporter. The NLS should drive nuclear accumulation; adding the NES should shift it cytoplasmic, and leptomycin B should reverse that shift.
cards.quote: Attach each candidate signal to a large inert reporter, such as a multi-GFP fusion that diffuses only slowly.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: Design a direct test of whether Protein Z shuttles between nuclei rather than merely accumulating after synthesis.
cards.back: Fuse cells so two nuclei share cytoplasm, block new protein synthesis, and track Z from a labelled to an unlabelled nucleus; alternatively, photoactivate nuclear Z and watch it leave.
cards.quote: Fuse cells so two nuclei share one cytoplasm, block new protein synthesis and ask whether Z moves from a labelled nucleus to an unlabelled one.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: Which controls strengthen the claim that leptomycin B changes Protein Z localization specifically through CRM1 inhibition?
cards.back: Check cell health, include a known CRM1 cargo, and, if possible, rescue the phenotype with a leptomycin-resistant CRM1 mutant.
cards.quote: Check cell health, include a known CRM1 cargo, and, if available, rescue with a leptomycin-resistant CRM1 mutant.
cards.section: Predict and design: the drug puzzle

cards.front: Why is a dominant FG-domain mesh radius of about 2.6 nm not a universal nuclear-pore hole size?
cards.back: It is a model-dependent description from permeabilized HeLa cells, and the model also includes a small fraction of wider channels.
cards.quote: That is a model-dependent description, not a literal universal hole size.
cards.section: The pore is not one fixed mesh

cards.front: What observation argues that the nuclear-pore scaffold is not rigid?
cards.back: Fission-yeast pores constricted reversibly during energy depletion and hypertonic stress.
cards.quote: fission-yeast pores constricted reversibly during energy depletion and hypertonic stress
cards.section: The pore is not one fixed mesh

cards.front: To which cytoskeletal protein family do lamins belong?
cards.back: The intermediate-filament family.
cards.quote: Lamins belong to the intermediate-filament family.
